blocks.text: Which route to pick: menu, shortcut, or address bar

Chrome gives you three routes into the same dialog. The three-dot menu is the one Google documents, so start there the first time. The keyboard shortcut is faster once your fingers know it. The address bar is the backup when you cannot find the menu item or prefer typing. All three open the same Delete browsing data options, so the route you pick does not change what gets deleted. Google's help page lists the same steps for Mac, Windows, and Linux.

items: Three-dot menu: best the first time, because every step is visible.
⌘ ⇧ Delete: best once you use it often, because it skips the menu.
Address bar: best when you cannot find the menu item or prefer typing.

blocks.text: What the dialog clears, item by item

The dialog is a list of checkboxes, and each box controls one kind of stored data. Google's help page says to select Cookies and other site data, then check any other items you want removed. Older guides for Chrome on Mac describe the same dialog with two tabs, Basic and Advanced. The Basic tab covers browsing history, cookies and other site data, and cached images and files. The Advanced tab adds passwords, autofill data, site settings, and hosted app data. Google's current help does not name those tabs, so trust what your screen shows over any guide, including this one.

rows: The list of pages you visited
Sign-ins and site preferences that websites stored
Stored copies of images and pages that load faster
Saved names, addresses, and form entries
Per-site permissions such as camera or location

blocks.title: Read the list first
blocks.text: Passwords and autofill can sit in the same dialog as cookies. Untick them unless you mean to remove them. Think before you click Delete data, because this dialog cannot restore what it removes.
Choose a time range that matches the problem

The time range dropdown sets how far back Chrome deletes. Google's help page gives two examples, Last hour and All time. Your dropdown may show more options than these two. Pick the range that matches the problem, not the one that feels safest. A wide range removes more, so you may need to sign in to more sites afterward.
Match the range to the symptom. A page that broke today points to Last hour. A login loop that started weeks ago points to a wider range, or to All time if nothing else helps.

Here is a worked example. A bank page shows an error right after a password change. Clear cookies for the last hour, reload the page, and sign in again. If the error stays, run the same dialog again with All time. Each run only touches the range you picked, so the first attempt works as a low-cost test.
Keyboard shortcut to clear browsing data on Mac: ⌘ ⇧ Delete

Google's keyboard shortcuts page lists ⌘ ⇧ Delete as the way to open the Delete Browsing Data options on Mac. Make sure Chrome is the active app, then hold Command and Shift and press Delete. The shortcut is handy when you are mid-task and do not want to reach for the trackpad. It only opens the dialog. You still pick the time range, tick the boxes, and click Delete data.

blocks.title: If the shortcut does nothing
blocks.text: Check that Chrome is the front app and that you hold both modifier keys. If nothing happens, open the three-dot menu and choose Delete browsing data instead.
Clear data from the address bar

Chrome's address bar does more than load sites. Click it and type Delete browsing data. Chrome offers an Action chip in the suggestions. Select that chip, and the same dialog opens. Google's help page documents this route, so it is a supported way in. Use it when you are already typing and the menu feels far away.
Incognito is not the same as clearing data

People mix these two up. Incognito opens with ⌘ ⇧ N, according to Google's keyboard shortcuts page. An Incognito window keeps your session separate from the rest of Chrome. Clearing data does something else. It removes what Chrome already stored. If you want today's history gone, clear it. If you want to browse without leaving more history behind, open Incognito. You can use both on the same day for different reasons.
What clearing cookies changes for you

Cookies are how many sites remember you. They keep sign-in details and some site preferences. When you clear them, sites forget that you logged in. Expect a sign-in page on email, shopping, and bank sites. Saved language choices and some display settings can reset too. That is the trade-off for a clean slate.

Say Gmail keeps opening the wrong account. You clear cookies from the last hour, reload Gmail, and choose the right account. The fix takes a few minutes, and the only cost is one more sign-in. If you clear All time instead, expect to sign in to every site you use, which is a bigger job.
Chrome and macOS versions you need

The steps in this guide follow the wording in Google's current Chrome help, which uses Delete browsing data and Delete data. A third-party tracker, WhatIsMyBrowser, lists the latest Chrome for macOS as version 156.0.8078.82, released 4 November 2026. Google's own release notes did not confirm that build number, so treat it as a tracker figure. If your menu shows different labels, your Chrome build may be older.

Chrome 150 is the last release that supports macOS 12 Monterey, according to 9to5Google, which quotes Google. Chrome 151 requires macOS 13 Ventura or newer. Google's Chrome Enterprise requirements page also lists macOS 13 Ventura and up as the minimum for Mac. Older Chrome versions keep working on Monterey, but they stop getting updates. 9to5Google reported a tentative July 28, 2026 release date for Chrome 151, so check Google's schedule for current dates.
Common mistakes when clearing browsing data

items: Ticking every box without reading the list. Passwords and autofill can go with cookies.
Expecting Incognito to erase earlier history. It only keeps new sessions separate.
Choosing Last hour when the problem started last week. Older data stays in place.
Following an old Customize menu path. Current Chrome says Delete browsing data.
Skipping the reload test. Without it, you cannot tell which item fixed the problem.

blocks.text: If a site still shows old data after you clear it, reload the page, then close the tab and open it again. Clearing removes stored data, but an open tab may still show what loaded before. If the site behaves the same way, run the dialog once more with a wider range.
What to do after you clear data

Start with the site that caused the problem. Sign in again if it asks, and check the account name before you continue. If you cleared data on a shared Mac for privacy, sign out of accounts you do not want left open before you hand the machine over. Then repeat the reload test so you know the fix held. Next time, try Last hour first. It keeps the cleanup small and easy to check.

faq.question: Does clearing browsing data in Chrome delete my passwords?
faq.answer: Only if you tick the passwords box. Older Chrome guides list passwords under an Advanced tab in the same dialog. Read the checkboxes before you click Delete data, and untick anything you want to keep.

faq.question: Will clearing cookies sign me out of websites?
faq.answer: Often, yes. Cookies hold many sign-in details, so sites that remember you will ask you to sign in again. Have your passwords ready for email and bank sites.

faq.question: What is the keyboard shortcut to clear browsing data on Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⌘ ⇧ Delete while Chrome is the active app. Google's shortcut list says it opens the Delete Browsing Data options. You still choose a time range and the items to delete.

faq.question: Is Incognito the same as clearing browsing data?
faq.answer: No. Incognito, opened with ⌘ ⇧ N, keeps a session separate. Clearing removes data that Chrome already stored. Use each one for a different job.

faq.question: Why can't I find Delete browsing data in my menu?
faq.answer: Chrome menus change between versions. Older guides describe a Customize menu with Settings and Advanced. If that is your layout, type Delete browsing data in the address bar and select the Action chip.

faq.question: Do these steps work on Windows or Linux?
faq.answer: Google's help page lists the same steps for Chrome on Mac, Windows, and Linux. The Mac shortcut is ⌘ ⇧ Delete. Look up the Windows and Linux shortcut on Google's shortcut page before you use it.

faq.question: Can I clear browsing data on macOS 12 Monterey?
faq.answer: Yes, the installed version still works. Chrome 150 is the last release that supports macOS 12, according to 9to5Google. Older installs keep working, but they stop receiving updates.

steps.name: Open the three-dot menu
steps.text: Open Google Chrome on your Mac and look at the top right of the window. Click the three-dot More menu, just past the address bar. This is the menu that holds Delete browsing data.
steps.tip: The three-dot menu lives in the Chrome window. It is not in the Mac menu bar at the top of the screen.

steps.name: Choose Delete browsing data
steps.text: Click Delete browsing data in the menu. Chrome opens the Delete browsing data dialog. Nothing is deleted yet. You choose the options first.
steps.tip: The shortcut opens this same dialog, so you can skip the menu once you know it.

steps.name: Pick a time range
steps.text: Open the time range dropdown. Choose Last hour to clear only recent data, or All time to clear everything. Your dropdown may list more options than these two.
steps.tip: Pick Last hour first if one site is misbehaving. You can always run the dialog again with a wider range.

steps.name: Tick the items you want gone
steps.text: Tick Cookies and other site data. Tick any other item you want removed, such as browsing history or cached images and files. Leave boxes unticked when you want to keep that data.
steps.tip: Read each box before you tick it. Passwords can sit in the same list.

steps.name: Click Delete data
steps.text: Click Delete data at the bottom of the dialog. Chrome removes the ticked items. Wait for the dialog to close before you go back to a site.

steps.name: Check the result
steps.text: Reload a site you use often. If you were signed in and cleared cookies, expect a sign-in page. If you still see old data, work through the troubleshooting list on this page.
steps.tip: Repeat the reload test after each run so you know which item made the difference.

troubleshooting.problem: Delete browsing data is missing from my menu.
troubleshooting.fix: Type Delete browsing data in the address bar and select the Action chip. Older guides describe a Customize menu, then Settings, then Advanced. Google's current wording is Delete browsing data.

troubleshooting.problem: Sites still remember me after I cleared data.
troubleshooting.fix: Check that you ticked Cookies and other site data and picked a wide enough time range. Then reload the site. Some pages may still show what loaded before, so close the tab and open it again.
This dialog cannot bring them back. Sign in again to each site, and check any password manager you use for a saved copy.
Make sure Chrome is the active app and that you hold Command and Shift with Delete. If it still fails, use the three-dot menu and Delete browsing data instead.

troubleshooting.problem: The dialog will not open from the menu.
troubleshooting.fix: Click an empty part of the Chrome window to make it the active app, then open the three-dot menu again.
